intro: In this college you'll learn how to understand rules and instructions, describe what happened in the past, talk about danger, and call the emergency number 112 to reach the police, the fire brigade or an ambulance.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — staying safe in Dutch
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme ten. Its title is a real question you will hear and ask in daily life: [[Is dat wel veilig?]], which means 'is that actually safe?'. That little word [[wel]] adds a note of doubt, like 'are you sure this is safe?'. This theme is about safety, accidents and emergencies. You will learn to follow rules, to say what happened, to warn people about danger, and most importantly to phone for help. These are not just words for an exam — one day they may help you protect yourself, your children or a stranger on the street. The key word for the whole theme is [[veilig]], which means 'safe', and its opposite [[gevaarlijk]], which means 'dangerous'. You will also hear [[het gevaar]], 'the danger', and [[voorzichtig]], 'careful'. A warm warning Dutch people say all the time is [[Wees voorzichtig!]], meaning 'be careful!'. As always, I explain everything in English, but every Dutch word and sentence you hear is spoken by a native Dutch voice, so you train your ear and your pronunciation at the same time. Try to listen closely and repeat each phrase out loud after me, even if it feels strange at first. Ready to begin? [[Laten we beginnen!]]

paragraphs.heading: Rules: moeten, mogen and niet mogen
paragraphs.text: First, the rules. In the Netherlands you see signs and hear instructions everywhere, and three little verbs do most of the work. The first is [[moeten]], which means 'must' or 'have to'. For example, a sign or an official might tell you [[U moet hier stoppen.]], 'you must stop here'. The second is [[mogen]], which means 'may' or 'to be allowed to', as in [[U mag hier parkeren.]], 'you may park here'. The third is the same verb made negative: [[mogen niet]] or [[mag niet]], 'may not', 'are not allowed to'. So you might be told [[U mag hier niet parkeren.]], 'you may not park here'. These are modal verbs, and they follow a clear pattern: the modal verb takes second place in the sentence, and the main verb jumps to the very end as an infinitive. Listen: [[Je mag hier niet zwemmen, het is gevaarlijk.]], 'you may not swim here, it is dangerous'. On official signs you will also see one strong word: [[verboden]], which means 'forbidden'. If you read [[Roken verboden]], that simply means 'smoking forbidden'. When something is allowed, the friendly word is [[toegestaan]], 'permitted'. Learn this trio well — [[moeten]], [[mogen]], [[verboden]] — and you can read almost any rule in the country.

paragraphs.heading: What happened? The perfect tense
paragraphs.text: Now, how do you describe something that already happened? Dutch uses the perfect tense, and for this theme the single most important sentence is [[Wat is er gebeurd?]], which means 'what happened?'. Notice it uses [[is]], a form of 'to be', not 'to have'. That is because most Dutch verbs build the past with [[hebben]], 'to have', but verbs of movement or change use [[zijn]], 'to be'. The verb [[gebeuren]], 'to happen', is one of them, so you say [[Er is een ongeluk gebeurd.]], 'an accident has happened'. Another vital one is [[vallen]], 'to fall', which becomes [[gevallen]]. So you can report [[Mijn buurman is van de trap gevallen.]], 'my neighbour fell down the stairs'. For most other verbs you use 'have': [[Ik heb alles gezien.]], 'I saw everything', and [[Ik heb 112 gebeld.]], 'I called 112'. To tell your story in order, three small words help enormously: [[eerst]] for 'first', [[toen]] for 'then', and [[daarna]] for 'after that'. Listen to a tiny story: [[Eerst hoorde ik een harde klap.]] [[Toen zag ik twee auto's op de weg.]] [[Daarna heb ik meteen 112 gebeld.]] That is 'first I heard a loud bang, then I saw two cars on the road, after that I immediately called 112'.

paragraphs.heading: Talking about danger
paragraphs.text: Let's talk about danger itself, because warning someone clearly can save them. The strongest word you can shout is [[Dat is levensgevaarlijk!]], which means 'that is life-threatening!' — literally 'life-dangerous'. A calmer version is [[Dat is heel gevaarlijk.]], 'that is very dangerous'. To warn a person gently, you say [[Pas op!]], meaning 'watch out!', or the longer [[Pas goed op jezelf.]], 'take good care of yourself'. If there is a fire, the word is [[de brand]], and you might cry [[Brand! Bel de brandweer!]], 'fire, call the fire brigade!'. Other key danger words are [[het ongeluk]], 'the accident'; [[gewond]], 'injured'; and [[het slachtoffer]], 'the victim'. When something is broken or unsafe, you can say [[Dit is kapot en gevaarlijk.]], 'this is broken and dangerous'. In an emergency, staying calm matters as much as the words, so Dutch people say [[Blijf rustig.]], 'stay calm', and [[Geen paniek.]], 'no panic'. A lovely proverb captures the Dutch attitude to safety: [[Beter voorkomen dan genezen.]], which means 'prevention is better than cure'. And another reminds us accidents happen easily: [[Ongelukken zitten in een klein hoekje.]], 'accidents lurk in a small corner'. Knowing these phrases means you can both warn others and reassure them when things go wrong.

paragraphs.heading: Calling 112 and talking to the police
paragraphs.text: Here is the most practical part of the whole theme. In the Netherlands, the emergency number is [[honderdtwaalf]], written 1-1-2. You call [[112]] for the police, [[de politie]]; the fire brigade, [[de brandweer]]; or an ambulance, [[de ambulance]] — whenever there is real, urgent danger to life. When you call, the operator will ask which service you need with the question [[Politie, brandweer of ambulance?]]. Then they ask [[Wat is er gebeurd?]], 'what happened?', and crucially [[Waar bent u?]], 'where are you?'. So learn to say your location: [[Ik ben op de Kerkstraat in Utrecht.]], 'I am on Kerkstraat in Utrecht'. They may ask [[Is er iemand gewond?]], 'is anyone injured?'. Two more sentences are gold: [[Stuur snel een ambulance.]], 'send an ambulance quickly', and [[Kunt u de politie waarschuwen?]], 'can you alert the police?'. If you witnessed it, say [[Ik ben getuige.]], 'I am a witness'. Important Dutch tip: stay on the line until the operator says you may hang up, and speak slowly. If you are nervous, you may always say [[Ik spreek niet zo goed Nederlands.]], 'I do not speak Dutch very well' — the operators are trained to help. For non-urgent police matters, by the way, the number is 0900-8844, not 112.

paragraphs.heading: A real call — and well done
paragraphs.text: Let's put it all together with a short scene, so it lives in your ear. Imagine you see a cyclist hit by a car. You grab your phone and dial [[112]]. The operator answers: [[Alarmcentrale 112, wat is er gebeurd?]] — 'emergency centre 112, what happened?'. You stay calm and say: [[Er is een ongeluk gebeurd op de Kerkstraat.]] [[Een auto heeft een fietser geraakt.]] That is 'an accident has happened on Kerkstraat; a car hit a cyclist'. The operator asks [[Is de fietser gewond?]], 'is the cyclist injured?'. You answer [[Ja, zijn been doet veel pijn.]], 'yes, his leg hurts a lot'. The operator says [[Goed, ik stuur een ambulance. Blijf bij de man.]], 'alright, I'll send an ambulance, stay with the man'. You reply [[Dat doe ik. Dank u wel.]], 'I will, thank you'. Practise that little dialogue out loud today — it is exactly the Dutch you would need in a true emergency. You have now learned to follow rules, describe the past, warn about danger, and call for help. That is powerful, real-life Dutch. [[Heel goed gedaan!]] Well done — and please, [[wees voorzichtig]] out there. I will see you in the next theme!
